title: Su Shi Visits His Old Opponent Wang Anshi
text:
In 11th century Song China, Wang Anshi was the chief minister behind the sweeping reforms known as the New Policies. The poet and official Su Shi was one of their fiercest critics. The conflict divided the court for years, and Su's sharp tongue and pen made him enemies. In 1079 he was arrested over poems said to mock the government, nearly executed, and then exiled to Huangzhou.

By 1084 Wang Anshi had long since retired from power and was living quietly at Jinling, today Nanjing. That year Su Shi, given permission to move nearer the capital, traveled down the Yangtze and stopped there. According to Song accounts, the old statesman rode out on a donkey to meet him at the river. The two spent many days together, walking in the hills, discussing poetry and Buddhism, and writing poems to each other.

In one of the poems he wrote in reply to Wang, Su Shi said that the old man had urged him to buy a small plot of land and settle nearby, and that he now felt he had come to follow him ten years too late. Wang died two years later.
lesson: Political opponents can still recognize each other's worth once the fight is over. Do not let a past contest stop you from honoring a gifted adversary.
source: Su Shi, poems written in reply to Wang Anshi at Jinling (1084); Song period anecdotal accounts
caveat: Some anecdotes about their meeting, including the warmth of their words, come from later collections and may be embellished.
